summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics: tokens/sec per dollar, caching and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run dedicated perf benchmark and update cost model spreadsheet. Security docs to be shared for VPC questions.
transcript:
00:00 Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll kick off - this is our weekly POC sync for Lunaris, cost econ focus. quick roll call?
00:07 Maya Chen: Maya here.
00:10 Lukas Novak: Lukas on infra.
00:12 Sara Gomez: Sara - CTO.
00:15 Ravi Patel: Ravi from Redwood, I'll run through the perf asks.
00:20 Jamie Park: Cool. Quick agenda: one - go over the cost model updates; two - caching and batching outcomes from last run; three - actions, next steps.
00:30 Maya Chen: Sounds good. On the cost side we ran your spreadsheet w/ our traffic profile last night, saw some interesting numbers.
00:37 Lukas Novak: yeah the token distribution is heavy tail - a lot of short queries but a small slice of long context ones.
00:42 Jamie Park: perfect, that's typical. So high-level: tokens/sec per dollar depends on three levers - model choice/quantization, batching, and cache hit rate. the spreadsheet we've updated factors in dedicated pricing vs hosted with burst.
00:56 Ravi Patel: Right, and we ran two micro-benchmarks - one with prefix caching enabled at 60% hit and one without. With caching we saw effective tokens/sec per dollar improve ~2.3x on the short-ctx workload because we avoid regen for the same prompts.
01:12 Maya Chen: Wait 2.3x, is that across p99 latency too or just avg?
01:16 Ravi Patel: Good question - that's across average tokens/sec cost. p90 latency stayed within your SLO (~300ms per short request) when batching was modest, but p99 did increase slightly under high batching.
01:28 Sara Gomez: So we're trading off cost for tail latency if we push batching more aggressively?
01:32 Ravi Patel: Exactly. Batching increases throughput but can add queueing latency; on the workloads you gave, moving from batch size 8 to 32 improved tokens/sec by 1.8x but p99 grew by about 120ms.
01:45 Lukas Novak: Are those numbers for quantized kernels? we saw different perf on int8 vs fp16.
01:50 Ravi Patel: The baseline was 4-bit quantized model w/ optimized kernels; we included a fp16 run as comparison. Quantization reduced token compute cost by ~30% in our run, but quality regressions for some prompt types - we flagged those in the eval sheet.
02:04 Maya Chen: Hmm quality regressions are concerning for our user-facing assistant; we'd need to tie regen rates to business metrics.
02:10 Jamie Park: Totally. That's why we recommended trialing semi-quantized strategy - use quantized variants for background inference and keep fp16 or unq near the head for critical paths, or fallback on mismatch.
02:22 Ravi Patel: Also worth noting prefix/KV cache is most effective for sessions with repeated context - your product has high session reuse so the ~60% hit was realistic. That saved us tokens and compute.
02:34 Maya Chen: Lukas, do you have the cache hit numbers from our prod?
02:37 Lukas Novak: We pulled a week of telemetry - session-level prefix cache hit around 58% for top 5 intents, long tail lower. I'll send the CSV.
02:45 Jamie Park: Great. On the hosted vs dedicated question - dedicated gives you predictable tokens/sec capacity and slightly lower unit cost at scale, but requires commit and VPC plumbing.
02:56 Sara Gomez: Our main constraint is data residency and audit logs - we'd probably push for Private/VPC eventually. What's the delta on cost?
03:03 Ravi Patel: In our model sheet, dedicated at your committed level reduced token price by ~22% vs hosted at current rates, but you'd need to weigh the commit. Also dedicated lets you pin model variants and the kernel stack which helps tail latency.
03:17 Lukas Novak: For Private we need KMS/HSM integration and SAML for SSO. Can you share the SOC2 and network diagrams?
03:23 Jamie Park: Absolutely - we'll drop the SOC 2 report and VPC design doc in the shared folder after the call.
03:28 Maya Chen: On batching tradeoffs, can you show how dynamic batching might help? we worry about p99 for SLAs.
03:34 Ravi Patel: Dynamic batching gives you the best of both worlds - size adjusts to queue and latency. In our tests, dynamic batching kept p99 within ~50ms of baseline while still getting ~1.5x tokens/sec improvement. But it requires tuning thresholds.
03:47 Sara Gomez: If dynamic batching needs kernel-level changes, is that something Redwood will handle?
03:52 Ravi Patel: We manage the serving runtime tuning; we can iterate on thresholds and telemetry hooks. For kernel selection, we select optimized kernels automatically, but we may ask for permission to run perf tests on a sample to pick the best profile.
04:05 Maya Chen: OK - what do you need from us to run the dedicated perf benchmark you mentioned?
04:09 Ravi Patel: We need a synthetic workload: 100k tokens total across mixed short/long queries, plus the session reuse pattern (CSV), and expected RPS peaks. Lukas can provide telemetry extracts. Also we need a preferred date to run the benchmark.
04:21 Lukas Novak: I can generate the telemetry and the CSV by Tuesday.
04:24 Jamie Park: Great. We'll plan the benchmark for next Thursday if that works. Ravi to coordinate infra and share a runbook.
04:30 Maya Chen: Regarding the cost model spreadsheet, a few notes: include separate rows for cache-on vs cache-off, and include a conservative cache-hit scenario (40%). We want to see breakeven points.
04:40 Jamie Park: Noted - I'll update the sheet with 40/60/75% cache hit scenarios.
04:44 Ravi Patel: Also we'll add a sensitivity table for batch size and quantization combos - tokens/sec/$ vs p99 latency.
04:52 Sara Gomez: Any legal/procurement blockers we should be aware of?
04:55 Jamie Park: Nothing major - once you decide on Dedicated/Private we'll route to our legal. For now we can proceed with benchmarks and cost modeling.
05:03 Maya Chen: Cool. Quick recap?
05:05 Jamie Park: Recap: 1) Ravi runs perf benchmark with 100k token synthetic workload next Thursday; 2) Jamie updates cost sheet with cache scenarios & sends to Maya; 3) Lukas provides telemetry and cache hit CSV by Tue; 4) Redwood shares SOC2 + VPC docs; 5) follow-up sync after benchmark to review numbers and discuss commit.
05:25 Maya Chen: Fine by me. Thanks all.
05:30 Jamie Park: Thanks, talk soon.
05:33 call ended
